I  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


I.1 Products covered by this document

The product assessed in this document is referenced as GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_WAV_001_032 for the
global wave reanalysis describing past sea states over the years 1993-2022 for initial production, then
in interim mode for subsequent periods. Recently, time series have been extended backwards in time
to  1st January 1980. This product also bears the name of WAVERYS within the Global High Resolution
(GLO-HR) MFC, corresponding to other global multi-year products like GLORYS, BIORYS, etc. The core of
WAVERYS is based on the MFWAM model (Aouf & Lefèvre, 2015), a third-generation wave model that
calculates the wave spectrum, i.e., the distribution of sea state energy in frequency and direction on a
1/5° irregular grid. The wave parameters derived from the wave spectrum, such as significant wave
height (SWH) or the mean wave period, are delivered globally on a regular grid size of 1/5° with a 3-hour
time step. The wave spectrum is discretized into 30 frequencies obtained from a geometric sequence of
first member 0.035 Hz and a common ratio of 7.5. WAVERYS considers oceanic currents from the
GLORYS12 physical ocean reanalysis (Jean-Michel et al., 2021) and assimilates significant wave height
observed from historical altimetry missions and directional wave spectra from Sentinel 1 Synthetic
Aperture Radar (SAR) from 2016 onwards. For the 2020-time extension and onwards, wave spectra from
the SWIM (Surface Wave Investigation and Monitoring instrument)-CFO sat data are assimilated.



WAVERYS is described in Law-Chune et al. (2021) which also covers some of the results shown in this
document.


I.2 Summary of the results

The quality of the WAVERYS wave reanalysis was estimated by: (i) comparing SWH model predictions to
HY-2A satellite altimetry data (non-assimilated, open ocean, validation period of 2014-2018);  (ii)
comparing the mean wave parameters with Copernicus Marine in-situ buoy measurements (coastal
data, validation period 1994-2015); and (iii) comparing the dynamics of these mean parameters with
respect to ERA5 wave reanalysis for the entire period for which ERA5 data is available. The quality
assessment covers a subset of key wave parameters; results of which are summarized below.

Significant wave height (SWH): For the open sea, WAVERYS performs with a global scatter index (SI) of
8.5% with relatively low biases of about 2 cm. The quality of the analysis is better for tropical latitudes
than for high latitudes where SI exceeds 10%. This is particularly the case for coastal areas and/or those
subject to complex oceanic processes (e.g., current instabilities, tides, etc.), where SI can reach 20%.
Generally, the wave model performs worse in light wind conditions (typically summer) than in strong
wind conditions that effectively constrain the model (typically winter), with SI differing by a few percent.

Validation of the following quantities is only available for a limited set of coastal moorings located mainly
in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans of the Northern Hemisphere:

Peak wave period: Despite the known challenges posed by coastal areas to wave models, the bias in
peak periods are only about 10 milliseconds (ms). In an area along the Iberian coast and in the Azores,
SI reaches around 40% (compared to the average of 26% over all measurements).

Zero up-crossing period: Mean wave period bias is about 40 ms and SI remains low at about 15%.
WAVERYS is particularly efficient at capturing Pacific Ocean swells (scatter index of 11% near Hawaii).

II  PRODUCTION SYSTEM DESCRIPTION


Production centre names: Mercator Ocean International and Météo-France

Production system name: GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_WAV_001_032 (or WAVERYS for short-name)

The CMEMS global wave reanalysis, WAVERYS, was built from the real-time wave system GLO-WAVE-
001-027. It therefore contains a similar wave physics and model configuration. The core of the system
is based on the wave model MFWAM, a third-generation wave model operated at Météo-France (Aouf
et al., 2021).

MFWAM uses the computing code of ECWAM-IFS-42R2 with a dissipation term developed by Ardhuin
et al. (2010) (known as “ST4 physics”) added with some improvements obtained from the European
research project “My Wave”. To be consistent with the latest version of the CMEMS global wave system,
the dissipation source term was also adjusted to reduce the surface stress at the air/sea interface for
high and intermediate winds (Rainaud et al., 2019). Typically, with these models, predicting the high
frequency part of the spectrum is tricky because these are the frequencies where wind energy is
transferred to feed the waves, but also the part of the spectrum subject to the most dissipative
processes. WAVERYS corrects the upper part of the spectrum (high frequencies) to a Phillips tail
(theoretical spectrum) to ensure realistic spectral content.

WAVERYS’s bathymetry  is generated by using 2-minute gridded global topography data from
ETOPO2/NOAA. The native model grid is irregular with latitudinal distances decreasing poleward. At the
equator, the distance in the latitudinal direction is fixed with a grid size of 1/5°. The wave spectrum is
discretized into 24 directions and 30 frequencies starting from 0.035 Hz and up to 0.58 Hz. A minimum
water depth is set to 5 m, which is more than sufficient at the 1/5° global resolution to represent shoaling
effects.

Generally, the quality of wave forecasts is severely constrained by surface winds, and the WAVERYS
wave reanalysis is driven by winds and ice-cover from the latest climate reanalysis produced at ECMWF,
namely ERA5 (Hersbach et al., 2020). ERA5 climate reanalysis has an average resolution of 31 km, and
although hourly analysis fields are available, three hourly winds are used in WAVERYS for consistency
with the other forcing data such as oceanic currents and data-assimilation. ERA5 reanalysis has
significantly improved the ERA-interim (ERAI) reanalysis. Appendix 1 provides an illustration of the
differences in results in terms of wind-sea modelled during a cyclonic event using ERAI and ERA5.

Producing a reanalysis involves using past observations of model variables to have the best possible
initial states for the forecast segments. Due to their large spatial coverage and high temporal
repetitiveness, significant wave height observations from satellite are crucial for operational models.
WAVERYS takes advantage of most historical altimetry missions. These data were reprocessed
(corrected and validated) by CERSAT-IFREMER. The assimilation of SWH is performed over the entire
period with a time step and an assimilation window of 3 hours. The assimilation system can use
conjointly SWH and  directional wave spectra provided by measurements from  satellites. The
assimilation of wave spectra consists in performing optimal interpolation on mean energy and
wavenumber components of dominant wave trains called partitions. Since March 2016, the level 2
Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) directional wave spectra from Sentinel-1A are provided by the European
Space Agency and are also assimilated to correct the low frequency part of the wave spectrum which
controls the swell partitions. WAVERYS is the first available global wave reanalysis that assimilates SAR
wave spectra measured from space. Since February 2020, SAR wave spectra from CFO-SAT are also
assimilated, also obtained for ESA CCI Sea State project (Dodet et al., 2020). The assimilation of these

Ocean currents can strongly impact wave propagation and induce a change in wave frequency, energy
and direction (Philipps, 1984). To provide the most accurate sea state, WAVERYS considers 3-hourly
surface   currents   provided   by   the   global   physical   reanalysis   of  CMEMS   called
GLORYS12V1(GLOBAL_REANALYSIS_PHY_001_030  CMEMS   product).  GLORYS12   currents   are
interpolated on the native grid of the wave model at 1/5°. This approach has shown very positive results
for wave fields interacting with high-energy current systems such as the Agulhas.

Note on wave spectra: Wave spectra are what the wave model calculates. They are often used to
compute all the average parameters that are distributed in CMEMS (significant height, period, partitions,
etc.). These wave spectra are not directly recorded along the model run because they are very heavy in
terms of data (24 directions × 30 frequencies × all grid points × output time steps). Wave spectra are
then lost during the production, but they are nevertheless recorded at a few sporadic points for
validation purposes. These few validation wave spectra are not disseminated within CMEMS.

III  VALIDATION FRAMEWORK


To measure the impact of the different forcing elements on the quality of wave forecasts, a series of
preliminary tests were carried out during the design of WAVERYS (see Appendix 2). These were intended
first to test the impact of ERA5 winds against ERAI winds, then to assess the addition of GLORYS currents
and the assimilation system separately. These tests were carried out for the year 2010. The SWH data
of the JASON2 altimeter was kept aside for validation purpose. The results can be found in appendix 2,
showing that the final solution for WAVERYS allows to obtain scatter index for the global open-sea below
10%; i.e., almost the same order of magnitude as the CMEMS real-time global wave system.

The wave model computes at each point of the domain grid the distribution of sea state energy
according to frequencies and propagation directions. This is what is called the local wave spectrum and
average wave parameters provided by CMEMS are derived from its shape and spectral moments. They
give to end-users practical and relevant information.



For the validation of WAVERYS, the following average wave parameters were considered:

    a)  Significant wave height (SWH) is probably the most important parameter because it corresponds
        to the estimate of wave height that would be made by a visual observer at sea. Physically, it
       represents the mean value of highest one-third of wave heights. Its validation tests the wave
       model's ability to distribute and disperse wind energy in frequency and direction, if the wind
        forcing is considered as correct. This quantity is approximated in the wave model from the
       zeroth moment of the wave spectrum.
    b)  Peak wave period (PWP) represents the period for which most of the energy is found. It is
       derived from the wave spectrum using the most energetic wave frequency.  Its quantity
       represents the way in which the wave model adjusts the energy across frequencies (balance
      between growth, dissipation, and wave-wave interactions).
    c)  Average zero-upcrossing period (TM10) represents the time between exceedances of mean
       water level on the front face of successive waves. This is the wave period classically derived from
       a temporal wave observation (from wave buoys). It can be approximated by a wave model using
       the second and zeroth moments of the wave frequency spectrum and represents the average
       frequency energy distribution.

    d)  Average wave direction (VMDR) represents the average direction where most of the wave
       energy propagates. It is connected to the model's ability to predict the energy distribution in
       terms of direction. It is approximated using the first directional moments of the wave spectrum.



The validation of WAVERYS is based on the direct comparison of the above quantities to three relevant
data sets.

    1.  The HY-2A satellite of the Haiyang series for SWH validation from 2013 onwards was used. HY-
      2A is China’s first ocean dynamic environment satellite and as it provides independent data for
      WAVERYS, it is well suited for validation purposes. This validation focuses on the large-scale and
        offshore ocean. The HY-2A SWH used in the validation are provided by the French Space Agency
        (CNES), which reprocessed the data recently (Jiang et al 2018). The Level 2 HY-2A wave data are
      downloaded from the users’ portal AVISO+ : https://www.aviso.altimetry.fr/fr/accueil.html
